# German ships as typed catalogs per locale, a prerendered answer page per locale, and a bilingual Template

Release 2 adds German to the app, the answer page, and emails ([research](../research/german-localization.md)).

- **Catalogs:** each catalog gets a `de.ts` beside the English one, typed so a missing key, an extra key, or a wrong `{placeholder}` fails typecheck. The message functions take the locale instead of the fixed `"en"`; plurals, dates, and numbers come from `Intl` for that locale.
- **Which language:** a Person's own setting, then the browser's languages, then the Organization's default. Emails render in the language stored with the send when it is created.
- **Answer page:** one prerendered page per locale (`/a`, `/de/a`), each loading only its own answer catalog. The Invitation link picks the page from the recipient's language. ADR 0008's budget applies to each page separately.
- **Words:** informal "du". Pulse and Team stay English; Round → Runde, Lead → Teamleitung, Organization → Organisation, Submission → Einsendung. Claude drafts, the product owner reviews in the PR.
- **Template:** the weekly team health Template ships in both languages; a new Pulse copies its Questions in the Lead's language. Existing Pulses keep their Questions.
- **Privacy:** the language is never stored with a Submission or an Answer. In a small Team it could single out the one German reader.

## Consequences

- The budget test runs per answer page.
- Pages rendered in `MainWorker.ts` (delivery time, unsubscribe) hold hard-coded English and must move to the catalog.
- Redaction gains German phone number cases.
- A Team with mixed languages sees the Pulse's Questions in the language they were created in.

# tasteskill 2.5

Build the website a good company would ship: it says plainly what is sold, shows the real thing on
every screen, and looks made for this client, not from a template and not like an art piece.
figma.com and x.ai are the bar (in words: `layout-v4.md` section 1).

`<skill>` is this folder. It needs Node 22+ and Chrome, Edge or Chromium (ffmpeg optional).

## House rules

These nine win over everything else in this skill.

1. **No caption or description under any image, render or visual.** Licence credits go in one
   footer line.
2. **Every visual renders, never an empty ground,** at 1440, 1024, 768 and 390.
3. **One section per screen:** the hero alone on the first screen, every section exactly one or
   two screens tall at 1440x900, no second section heading peeking in. The one exception is a
   live `photo-chapters` section, three or four screens, set by the moment.
4. **Equal left and right content edges.**
5. **Hover micro-animations:** a linked card lifts 2px, a photo zooms 1.02-1.03 inside its frame,
   buttons step on hover and press on click, underlines draw, card loops cycle in 2.5-4 s, repeat
   and restart on hover. The motion layer does it; never strip or override it. No tilt, carousels
   or timed tabs. Every hero enters once on load (`data-enter`), and every page carries one dealt
   moment, two on a long page (the gate holds both).
6. **More and better real photographs where they fit;** nicer backgrounds; better heroes, layouts
   and fonts.
7. **Real full-colour icons** (a known product's real icon, never a drawn one); small diagram
   visuals in cards (a hub with branches; one input, a main processor, three parallel lanes;
   pulses running along the lines).
8. **The big award-site scenes and creative moments are part of the skill:** every page deals its
   moments (photo- and type-led off tech), but shader effects and scenes only where the trade has a
   technical subject (tech, AI, developer tools, gaming, fintech, hardware), never on a local cafe,
   bakery, guesthouse or shop: those get photographs.
9. **Addresses:** street and district only (no street given: the district), no house number, postcode or coordinates; no register
   or VAT numbers; no phone in a real format; contacts on `.example`.

## 1. The kind of business decides everything

Write the kind on the plan's first line and declare it on the page: the page type on
`<html data-type>` and `<meta name="page-type">` (the same value), and `<meta name="site-kind">`;
a place adds `<meta name="page-kind" content="place">`. The dealers take the last column
(`start.mjs --page`, `moments.mjs --page`), the hero dealer the page type; `consistency.mjs` reads
the metas.

| Brief | page type | site-kind | kind |
|---|---|---|---|
| App, SaaS, AI, developer tool, fintech or banking app, a studio selling its own software | software | software | software |
| A game, a studio launching its game | software | gaming | gaming |
| Hardware or a tech device (a drone, a robot arm, a keyboard) | product | tech | tech |
| Any other physical product or brand (a chair, a bike, coffee beans sold online) | product | other | product |
| People are hired: clinic, law firm, agency, creative studio, trade | service | other | service |
| People come to it: cafe, bar, bakery, restaurant, guesthouse, small hotel, shop, florist, bike shop, gym, local studio | place | other | place |

A maker that also opens its door or teaches (a ceramics studio, a bakery with a web shop) is a
**place**; its web shop becomes the goods section. It is a product only when nothing happens at the door.

"Tech" below means site-kind software, gaming or tech; "other" is everything else. Effects,
scenes, loops, counts, CSS grounds, dark pages and dark heroes are tech only. An other page is
photographs, flat colour, type, real icons, the hero's entrance, its dealt moment (photo- or
type-led, `moments.md`) and the hover layer.

## 2. The page plan by kind

## 1. What SurveyBeat is

SurveyBeat measures how a team is doing, week over week, and helps the team act on what it learns.

A team lead sets up a short recurring check-in called a pulse. Each week (or each sprint, or each month), every member of the team gets a few questions. They answer in under a minute, usually without leaving their inbox or chat app. Once enough people answer, the team sees how it scored, how that compares with last time, and what people wrote. The lead and the team agree on one or two actions. The next pulse shows whether those actions helped.

The product loop has four steps, and every feature in this spec serves one of them.

1. **Ask.** A short, consistent set of questions reaches each member at a good time for them.
2. **Answer.** Answering is fast, works on a phone, and is safe. Members trust that anonymous really means anonymous.
3. **Understand.** The team sees trends, not single data points. Free-text comments are condensed into themes without exposing who wrote what.
4. **Act.** Findings turn into owned actions. The team sees the effect of those actions in later pulses.

The old product stopped at step 3, and step 3 was only half built. Most competitors also stop at step 3. The rebuild treats step 4 as a core feature.

### Who uses it

| Role | What they need |
| --- | --- |
| Team member | Answer in seconds. Be certain an anonymous answer cannot be traced back. See the team's results and what changed because of them. See their own answer history, privately. |
| Team lead | Set up a pulse once and never touch the schedule again. See a clear picture of the team's health, its trend, and what people are saying. Run a short team conversation about the results. Track actions. |
| Organization admin | Connect the company directory and single sign-on. Manage teams and leads. Set privacy policy for the whole organization. |
| Leadership viewer | See aggregated health across many teams without access to any team's individual responses or comments. |

### 5.1 Ask: set up and send pulses

- A lead can create a pulse in under two minutes by starting from a template. The product ships with templates for weekly team health, sprint retrospectives, onboarding check-ins (at 30, 60, and 90 days), and a manager feedback round.
- Question types are rating (1 to 5, with labeled ends), eNPS (0 to 10), single choice, multiple choice, short text, and long text. Each rating question can have an optional "Want to say more?" comment field.
- The question library is shared across the organization. Admins can mark questions as standard, so that every team asking the same question produces comparable data across the organization.
- The pulse editor shows an estimated answer time, and warns when a pulse goes over 7 questions or about 90 seconds.
- Optional rotation. A pulse can have a fixed core set of questions plus a rotating set, where each round asks one or two different questions. This covers more topics without making each round longer.
- Cadence uses each member's local time zone. Monday 9:00 means 9:00 for each recipient. A lead can skip a round (for holidays) or pause a pulse.
- Channels are email, Slack, and Microsoft Teams. Each member picks their preferred channel. Email is the fallback for everyone.
- The first question can be answered directly from the message. In email, each rating value is a link that opens the answer page with that value chosen; the answer is saved when the member confirms it there, because email security scanners open every link (ADR 0007). In Slack and Teams, the message has interactive buttons and, where the platform allows it, a modal for the rest.
- Reminders go only to members who have not answered, and there are at most two per round. A member can turn reminders off.
- A shareable link remains available for teams that do not use invitations. A link round cannot compute a response rate and cannot guarantee one answer per person. The UI says so.

### 5.2 Answer: the member experience

- The answer page loads in under one second on a mid-range phone on 4G. It needs no sign-in when opened from an invitation token. It does need sign-in when opened from the shared link, if the organization requires it.
- One question per screen on mobile. All questions on one page on desktop. Keyboard navigation works fully. The page meets WCAG 2.2 AA.
- The answer page states the round's anonymity mode in plain words before the first question, along with what the lead will and will not see. Example: "Your lead sees the team's combined answers once at least 4 people respond. Your name is never stored with your answers."
- A member can change answers until the round closes. In anonymous rounds this needs a design that does not link the person to the submission on the server. The recommended approach is a random edit key that only the member's browser stores. If the member loses the key, they cannot edit, and that is acceptable.
- After submitting, the member sees a thank-you screen and the team's current open actions. This reminds them that answering leads to change.
- A member has a private history page that shows their own past attributed answers. It also shows their anonymous answers if their browser still holds those edit keys. Nobody else can see this page.

# Anonymous Submissions store no person and no time, and are unlinkable at rest, not against a restore

**Threat model.** The Lead, Organization admins, and anyone using the product (UI, API, exports) must never be able to link a member to their Submission, and neither can an operator reading stored data, dumps, or R2 backups. We do **not** claim to defend against an operator who restores the Durable Object to a past moment (point-in-time recovery replays every write, including the one transaction that writes a Participation record and its Submission), reads Cloudflare's internal edge logs, or changes the code to start logging. Against that we use controls instead: only named people can trigger a restore, the privacy page states the 30-day restore window, and code changes on the submission path need review. The answer page's "Your name is never stored with your answers" is true of everything stored.

**Design.**
- Everything lives in the Organization's Durable Object. There is no per-Round object. The first Answer writes the Participation record and a Submission holding that one Answer in **one transaction**, which is how a double submission is rejected (a unique Participation record per Round and Person).
- An anonymous Submission stores only its Round, its Answers, and an Edit key hash. It stores **no person, no Invitation, and no time at all**, not even the day SPEC allows. A Participation record stores Round, Person, and the fact of answering, also with no time.
- Submission and Answer tables are `WITHOUT ROWID` with random 128-bit keys. Reads aggregate or sort by the random key. Dumps and backups are written in key order.
- **The anonymous Submission table has no person column, ever.** Attributed Submissions get their own table, so no bug can put a name on an anonymous answer.
- The Invitation token travels in the **URL fragment**, so the answer page GET (and every link scanner) never sends it. The page POSTs it to a **separate Submission Worker** with logs, traces, tail, Logpush, and Analytics Engine writes all off. That Worker logs error codes only. Tokens are stored only as hashes.
- The **browser generates the Edit key** and sends only its SHA-256 hash with the first Answer. Later Answers and changes carry only the Edit key. **No request may carry both an Invitation token and an Edit key**, and the server rejects one that does.

----
# Comments are redacted when stored, and the raw text is never kept

Release 1's rule-based redaction (ADR 0001) runs in the Submission Worker as the comment is saved. It uses the Organization's roster at that moment, and only the redacted text is stored. The raw text exists only in that request's memory. It is never logged, stored, or sent to a model. We rejected keeping the raw text and redacting each time a comment is shown, for two reasons. Deleting a Person would take their name out of the roster and expose it in every old comment that mentions them. And raw comments at rest would be the most identifying data SurveyBeat holds.

**What is removed:**
- first names, last names, full names, and email local parts of every Person in the Organization, matched as whole words, ignoring case, width, and accents (names shorter than 2 characters are ignored);
- email addresses, phone numbers (7 or more digits with common separators), @handles, and every URL.

Each match becomes a placeholder (`[name]`, `[email]`, `[phone]`, `[handle]`, `[link]`). A comment is never held back as a whole. Roster names that are also ordinary words ("will", "may") are redacted anyway.

## Consequences

- Redaction is permanent. A false positive can't be undone, and a member who edits their comment edits the redacted text.
- People added to the roster later are not redacted from older comments.
----
# Being an Organization admin grants no access to any Team's Results

The Organization admin role (WorkOS's org-level `admin`) covers administration only: Teams, Leads, and People. Seeing a Team's Results, comments, or Actions requires a Membership in that Team, whatever the person's Organization role. Admins are often the people members worry about most. If the admin role could read every Team's Results, it would undercut "trust before features" and put leadership roll-ups (Release 3) in through a side door.

> Extended by ADR 0014 (an Organization admin may add themselves to a Team).
---
# Comment themes are computed once at close, need two comments, never quote, and can't be edited

When a Round closes and meets the minimum group size, and the Organization has AI processing on (ADR 0015), the Organization Durable Object asks the model for at most 5 Comment themes over the Round's redacted comments (ADR 0009). Each theme is a short label and one neutral sentence. The model also returns which comments support each theme, and the object keeps only themes supported by **at least two comments**. The result is stored with the Round's Result and never recomputed.

**Who sees what.** Members see each theme's label and sentence, never raw comments and never counts. The Lead sees the themes, how many comments support each, and the redacted raw comments, as in Release 1. Comments that fit no theme with two supporters stay visible only to the Lead.

**No quotes.** The prompt and the JSON schema ask for paraphrase, and a check rejects any theme that repeats 6 or more consecutive words of a comment; a rejected theme is dropped, not repaired. Exact wording or a personal style can identify the author.

**Failure.** The call retries with backoff for up to 24 hours. Until it succeeds, Results show "Themes are being prepared"; after that, Results stand without themes. The Review window (#89) never waits for themes.

**No editing.** The Lead cannot edit, hide, or reorder themes. A Lead who could hide an unflattering theme before sharing would undercut trust before features (SPEC §3.1).

**What the page shows**
- **Opening section:** "Short, anonymous check-ins for your team" with one hard fact: 3 to 7 questions by email, a one-tap first answer, and results only once at least 4 people have answered. Beside it is a mock-up built from the app's real parts: the Invitation email with its 1–5 rating and a Result card.

- **Anonymity** (dark section): no name and no time stored on an anonymous Submission, nothing shown below 4 answers, comments redacted before they're saved, and admins see no Results. I checked each claim against the ADRs, and the reviewer checked them again.
- **Results:** themes, the discussion guide, the Lead's Note, and Actions that come back in the next Round.
- **Closing panel** and a footer with the language switch. English is at `/`, German at `/de/`.

The page has no JavaScript. It is built from the message catalogs at build time, and its "Sign in" and "Start a Pulse" links go to `/app`, which sends people to the app on that stage.

# GitButler CLI Skill

Use GitButler CLI (`but`) as the default version-control interface.

## Start Here

Choose the narrowest first command by task; avoid ritual status checks:

```bash
# Selected dirty files/hunks:
but diff

# Commit order, branch/stack placement, conflict overview:
but status

# File IDs, per-commit files, amend details:
but status -fv

# What one applied branch or commit changed, for review:
but diff <branch-or-commit>

# Details for one known branch or commit:
but show <id>
```

Do not run plain `but status` and then `but status -fv` unless the compact output lacks file details needed for the task.

For "commit just/only/specific changes on a new branch", use the fast path:

```bash
but diff
but commit -b <branch> -m "<msg>" <id> <id>
```

`but commit -b <branch> ...` creates the branch when it does not exist and prints the created commit. Do not run a separate `but branch new`, status command, or verification diff unless the task needs workspace information that the result does not provide.

In a linked worktree, such as `.claude/worktrees/*`, omit `-b` so the commit goes on the branch the worktree has checked out. Use that branch as the new branch; do not stack another one on it.

## IDs

The first token on each `but diff` / `but status` line is that line's ID. When a command needs an ID, copy it exactly from the current output; never hardcode or invent one. ID lifetimes differ by entity:

- Changes and sources are **positional, space-separated** IDs (`but commit -b feat -m "msg" uvw:2e4 uvw:e2c`). An uncommitted hunk ID is written `<file-id>:<hunk-id>` (e.g. `uvw:2e4`, copied from bare `but diff`) — the part after the colon is the hunk's ID, **not** a line range (`uvw:16-40` is invalid). Do not invent flags like `--changes` / `--hunk` / `--ids`, pass a line range, or comma-separate IDs — `uvw,qyo` is parsed as one ID and fails.
- `but diff` is the exception: it accepts at most **one** target. Bare `but diff` shows all uncommitted files; inspect committed files or other entities one target at a time — never `but diff <id> <id>`.
- A committed file is `<commit-id>:<file-id>` (e.g. `mzm:uvw`, shown under each commit). A committed hunk is `<commit-id>:<file-id>:<hunk-id>` and is shown by `but diff <commit-id>`. `@` means the uncommitted area.
- Commit IDs are stable change IDs that survive history edits (`amend`, `squash`, `move`, `uncommit`, `reword`). Commits without a change ID (e.g. upstream-only) lead with a sha prefix instead, and `#N`-suffixed refs disambiguate duplicates — both go stale after history edits, and a stale sha can silently resolve to the wrong commit. The `(sha …)` on verbose commit lines is informational — do not pass it to commands.
- Branch short IDs are snapshot-local selectors. Use full branch names for branch-targeting mutations; short IDs are safe only for immediate read-only inspection.
- File/hunk IDs copied from one diff read generally remain usable across chained commits. If one stops resolving, re-read `but diff` and retry.

**Chaining:** mutation output is concise by default, so you may chain mutations with `&&` off one inspection read. Do not chain branch short IDs through mutations; use full branch names. Add `--status-after` only when the next step needs workspace IDs or details that the mutation result does not provide. Chained `but commit` calls stack in the order written — the first is oldest, each later one goes on top. History edits may run in sequence when every commit ref involved is a change-ID ref; run them one at a time with `--status-after` when a ref is sha-based or `#N`-suffixed, or when the next command needs freshly issued IDs. Chaining `but uncommit <id> && but diff` is safe because bare `diff` needs no ID from the uncommit output. Never pipe a mutation through `tail` or `head`: the pipeline then exits with their status, so the next `&&` runs even when the mutation failed.

## Non-Negotiable Rules

1. Use `but` for all write operations. Never run `git add`, `git commit`, `git push`, `git fetch`, `git pull`, `git checkout`, `git merge`, `git rebase`, `git stash`, or `git cherry-pick`; `but pull --check` fetches. The only exceptions are selecting a side of a conflicted submodule in resolution mode (see Resolve conflicted commits) and creating a missing target branch (see Notes). If the user says a `git` write command, translate it to `but` and run that.
2. Mutation commands print their result without appending workspace status. Add `--status-after` only when the next step needs resulting workspace IDs or details; otherwise trust the mutation result and do not run a verification status/diff.
3. Branches marked `(merged upstream)` have landed; start new work on another branch. That marker alone does not mean `but pull` removes them: run `but pull --check` first. `but pull` removes only branches listed `[integrated]` ("has been integrated upstream and removed locally", or "has been merged into <target> and removed" when the target has no upstream) and rebases the rest, which stay applied. To clear a landed branch that stays applied, use `but unapply <branch>` (acts on its whole stack) rather than `but discard`. `push` and mutations (`commit`, `amend`, `squash`, `uncommit`, `reword`, `move`) refuse landed branches and commits, `absorb` skips them with a notice, and `commit` skips them when picking a default target.
4. Keep going between routine `but` commands. Put any status note in the same message as the next command, and don't end a turn on a summary that announces the next `but` step without running it. Finish with a concise summary.
5. Prefer this skill and `but skill reference` over exploratory help calls. Use `<command> --help` when required syntax is missing or a command fails; use top-level help only when you genuinely need to discover an undocumented command.
6. Other agents may share this checkout, so `@` can hold their edits. Commit, amend, and discard only the IDs or paths you changed. Bare `but commit`, `but absorb`, `but discard @`, and `git stash` take their work too, and a refusal naming files you didn't edit means you selected theirs.

## Command Patterns

- Initialize a Git repository: `but init` (current directory) or `but -C <path> init`. Non-interactive; creates no commits, remotes, or GitButler workspace. Existing repositories are left unchanged. In a repository with no commits, make the first commit with a bare `but commit -m "<msg>"`; `-b` is refused there.

- Commit: `but commit -b <branch> -m "<msg>" <id> <id>` — `-b <branch>` creates the branch if it does not exist
- Commit everything uncommitted: `but commit -b <branch> -m "<msg>"` (omit the IDs)
- Several commits from one diff: chain `but commit` calls with `&&` (commits stack oldest-first)
- Never pass `-s` to `commit`, `move`, or `pick`: it is `--switch`, not git's `--signoff`, and it unapplies every other stack.
- The branch is never positional (`but commit <branch>` fails; use `-b`), `but amend` always needs `-t`, and `but diff` takes one target (use a shared `dir/` or one call each).
- Commit at a specific history position: `--above <commit-or-branch>` or `--below <commit-or-branch>` (mutually exclusive). With a branch target, add `-b <new-name>` to name the new branch; otherwise its name is generated. The name must not already exist. Do not combine `-b` (even without a name) with commit/worktree targets.
- Targeting is **required** when more than one **stack** is applied; without it `but commit` fails with "Unclear where to commit. Found more than one stack". Several branches stacked together count as one stack — an untargeted commit then silently lands on the stack's top branch, so pass `-b` whenever the branch matters.
- Always pass `-m "<msg>"` (or `-F -` with a heredoc, `-F <file>` with a file outside the repository, or `--no-message`) to `but commit`, and to `but squash` whenever its sources are commits or branches unless the target is `@` (squash also takes `-u` to keep the target's message) — those compose a new message; without a flag an agent run keeps whatever the command composed (empty for `but commit`, the joined source messages for `but squash`) and a terminal opens an editor. Squash sources that are uncommitted or committed changes reuse the target's message and need no flag; squashing into `@` rejects message flags outright.
- Amend: `but amend -t <commit-or-branch> <file-or-hunk-id> <file-or-hunk-id>` — a branch target resolves to its newest commit
- Uncommit: `but uncommit <commit-id>` (whole commit), `but uncommit <branch>` (all commits and remove branch), `but uncommit <commit-id>:<file-id>` (committed file), or `but uncommit <commit-id>:<file-id>:<hunk-id>` (committed hunk); committed files and hunks may be mixed, but all must come from one commit
- Copy commits (sources stay unchanged): `but pick <sha> [<sha>...] -b <new-branch>` puts the copies on a new independent branch from the target, `-b <existing-branch>` on that applied branch's tip, and `--above <branch> -b <new-name>` (or `--below`) on a new branch stacked there. Pick applies sources in the order given, so pass them oldest first. For a branch that is not applied, list SHAs with `git log --reverse <target>..<branch>` and inspect them with `git show` or `but show <sha>`; `but diff` and the IDs that `but branch show` prints for it do not work.
- Move committed changes into an existing commit or `@`: `but squash <commit-id>:<file-id> -t <commit-id-or-@>` for a committed file; `but squash <commit-id>:<file-id>:<hunk-id> -t <commit-id-or-@>` for a committed hunk; all sources must come from one commit
- Move committed changes into a new commit at a chosen position: `but move <commit-id>:<file-id> --above <commit-or-branch> -m "<msg>"` for a committed file; `but move <commit-id>:<file-id>:<hunk-id> --above <commit-or-branch> -m "<msg>"` for a committed hunk (`--below`, `--branch`, and `--unstack` also work)
- `but split` and a `but move` of committed changes name their new commit with `-m` or `-F` too; without either the commit gets an empty message. `but move` rejects `-m`/`-F` for whole-commit and branch sources.
- Move commit to branch top: `but move <commit-id> -b <branch>`
- Move commits or committed changes onto a new named branch: `but move <source> --above <branch> -b <new-name>` (`--below` also works); use `but move <source> --unstack -b <new-name>` for an independent branch. Omit `-b` for a generated name. Naming is not supported when stacking or unstacking a branch source.
- Discard: `but discard <id> [<id>...]` — accepts branches, commits, committed changes, uncommitted changes, or `@` for all uncommitted changes
- Push: `but push <top-branch>` — pushes the selected branch and its ancestors; to update a stack, select its top branch once and never loop. Bare `but push` pushes all unpushed work when run non-interactively — one push per stack (its topmost unpushed branch, ancestors included), and the output lists every branch it pushed. It exits non-zero if any stack failed; stacks that already pushed stay pushed, and rerunning after fixing the failure is safe (up-to-date stacks are skipped). `but push` and `but pr new` replace the remote branch: if others may have pushed to it, bring their commits in first (see Bring in commits pushed to a branch's own remote).
- Create PR: `but pr new <branch-name> [-m "Title..."] [-F - | -F <file>] [-t] [--draft]` — auto-pushes first; do not run `but push` before it

## Task Recipes

### Update workspace from main

For "get latest from main", "update/sync this workspace", "rebase onto main", or "pull main":

1. `but pull` — one command; no preflight needed. Its output reports the resulting state, and `but undo` reverts it. Uncommitted changes that conflict with the update get conflict markers and show as `{conflicted}`; resolve them as in Conflicts in uncommitted files.
